title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Setting and problem. Euler is computing the first variation of J = ∫Z dx, where dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + … and p = dy/dx, q = dp/dx. The variation splits into an integral part (the Euler–Lagrange expression) and a 'second part', the endpoint term. The near curve starts at A and does not end at the principal endpoint M. In §40 (previous page) it ends first at μ, a vertical displacement Mμ = δy, and then at a nearby point ω whose abscissa is advanced by Pp = dx. Its endpoint contribution is Mμ·E + Z·Pp, where E = P − dQ/dx + ddR/dx² − … is the boundary coefficient of δy (in modern terms the generalized momentum ∂F/∂y' − d/dx ∂F/∂y'' + …).

This page (§41). Draw MO parallel to the axis. Then om = p·Pp, so the total rise is Oω = Mμ + p·Pp, and the slope of the chord Mω is s = Mμ/Pp + p. Let ω also denote the angle between Mω and the curve's tangent Mm. By the tangent subtraction formula, tan ω = (s − p)/(1 + sp) = Mμ/(Pp(1+p²) + p·Mμ). Inverting gives Mμ = Pp(1+p²)tan ω/(1 − p tan ω). The endpoint variation becomes Pp[Z + (1+p²)tan ω/(1 − p tan ω)·E].

§42. Euler asks for the direction at M along which the endpoint may slide with zero first variation. Setting the bracket to zero gives tan ω = Z/(pZ − (1+p²)E). Rewriting with the slope s, the condition is Z + (s − p)E = 0. This is exactly the modern transversality condition F + (φ' − y')F_{y'} = 0 for an endpoint free on a curve with slope φ'; here it is applied to the transversal direction itself.

Euler singles out the case where this direction is normal to the extremal (tan ω = ∞), i.e. pZ − (1+p²)E = 0. He reads it as a condition on the integrand Z. On the next page (§43) he solves it for Z = Z(x,y,p): pZ = (1+p²)Z_p, so Z = V(x,y)√(1+p²). He then interprets ∫V√(1+p²)dx as travel time with speed 1/V. This is the theorem that transversality coincides with orthogonality exactly for Fermat/isotropic-type integrands.
errors: No computational errors. The tangent-subtraction step, the inversion for Mμ and the solution for tan ω all check out.

Minor gap for higher-order integrands (Q, R ≠ 0). The endpoint term should also contain contributions from δp, δq at the end, e.g. (Q − dR/dx)δp + Rδq. Euler keeps only the δy coefficient P − dQ/dx + ddR/dx². So the general formula for ω is complete only in the first-order case. Euler immediately restricts to Q = R = 0 on the next page, where everything is correct.
Euler writes the curve's slope as 'tangens anguli mMo = p' and uses 'proxime' (to first order). This is fine for a first-variation argument.

ideas.what: Endpoint variation when the terminal point moves to a nearby point ω, combining the vertical variation Mμ and the extension Pp: δJ = E·δy + Z·δx with δy measured at fixed x
ideas.modern_name: general first-variation formula with variable endpoint
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and Lagrange (1750s–1760s); systematized in 19th-century textbooks
ideas.where_published: E420 itself, §§39–41; endpoint problems also in Euler's Methodus inveniendi (1744) and Lagrange's 1760 Miscellanea Taurinensia memoir

ideas.what: Direction at the endpoint along which the endpoint may slide with zero first variation: tan ω = Z/(pZ − (1+p²)E), equivalently Z + (s − p)F_p = 0
ideas.usually_credited_to: The condition for an endpoint on a given curve goes back to Euler/Lagrange; the name 'transversal' and the theory of transversals to A. Kneser (1900)
ideas.where_published: E420 (Novi Commentarii 16, 1771/72); unsure whether Euler earlier phrased it as an angle to the extremal

ideas.what: Characterization of integrands for which the transversal is always normal to the extremal: pZ = (1+p²)Z_p, hence Z = V(x,y)√(1+p²), interpreted as time of travel with speed 1/V
ideas.modern_name: transversality equals orthogonality iff the Lagrangian is conformally Euclidean (isotropic, Fermat-type metric); the rays-orthogonal-to-wavefronts property (Malus–Dupin/Hamilton) in variational form
ideas.usually_credited_to: Usually stated without attribution in Bolza/Bliss-type textbooks as a property of Fermat-type integrands; the optical theorem goes to Malus (1808), Dupin, and Hamilton (1828)
ideas.where_published: E420 §§42–43; unsure whether it appears elsewhere in Euler

missed.claim: Euler (1772) derives that the zero-variation endpoint direction is perpendicular to the extremal exactly when pZ − (1+p²)Z_p = 0. He solves this to get Z = V(x,y)√(1+p²) and gives the optical/brachistochrone time interpretation. This is the classical fact that transversality reduces to orthogonality only for isotropic (Fermat) integrands. Textbooks state it unattributed, and histories of transversality start with Kneser. Euler's priority for this characterization is, as far as I know, not commonly noted (unsure whether Goldstine discusses it).
missed.quote: Hic casus prae caeteris omnino notatu dignus considerari meretur, quo recta Mω fit ad curuam principalem in puncto M normalis, quod euenit, si fuerit p.Z − (1+pp)(P − dQ/dx + ddR/dx² etc.) = 0
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It gives Euler a precursor role in the theory of transversals and fields of extremals, and a variational route to the isotropic-medium wavefront orthogonality usually credited to Malus/Hamilton.

missed.claim: Euler builds the transversal direction as the locus of endpoints with zero endpoint variation, and ties its orthogonality to travel-time integrals. Implicitly this links the calculus of variations with Huygens-type wavefront geometry: Mω is an element of the 'wavefront' of the time function J. Euler does not develop the field-of-extremals or eikonal picture that Hamilton and Kneser later did.
missed.quote: quare hoc angulo ita constituto pro omnibus lineis proximis vbicunque in recta Mω terminatis variatio ex secunda parte oriunda euanescet
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical precursor of Hamilton–Jacobi/Kneser transversality theory. It is mainly of historiographical interest, not new mathematics.

missed.claim: Euler writes the general angle formula including higher-order terms (Q, R). He then solves the orthogonality condition only for first-order Z. The higher-order transversality question is left unexamined, and it would need the omitted δp boundary terms anyway.
missed.quote: tang. ω = Z/(pZ − (1+pp)(P − dQ/dx + ddR/dx² etc.))
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is minor; transversality for higher-order problems is standard today.

deep.surprise_reason: The transversality computation is routine for Euler. However, the explicit characterization that the transversal is normal exactly for Z = V(x,y)√(1+p²), with its optical-time reading, is a clean early statement of a result usually treated as folklore or tied to Kneser/Hamilton. Its Euler attribution seems underappreciated, though I cannot rule out that Goldstine or the Opera omnia notes record it.
transcription_corrections: The line 'ωMm = tang. ω = …' should be read as 'tang. ωMm = tang. ω = Mμ/(Pp(1+pp) + Mμ.p)', i.e. the tangent of the angle ωMm; the image is ambiguous but the mathematics requires the tangent.
Otherwise the transcription matches the image. 'tang. ωMo = Mμ/Pp + p' and the final condition 'p.Z − (1+pp)(P − dQ/dx + ddR/dx² etc.) = 0' are correct.
